title: Relative disk homotopy extension along a weak homotopy equivalence
statement: Use path components and continuous based homotopy groups as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Let $A,B$ be arbitrary topological spaces and $w:A\to B$ a continuous map inducing a bijection on path components and isomorphisms $\pi_j(A,a)\to\pi_j(B,w(a))$ for every $a\in A$ and $j\geq1$. Let $n\geq0$, put $D^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2\leq1\}$ and $S^{n-1}=\partial D^n$ (so $D^0$ is a point and $S^{-1}=\varnothing$), and give all products the ordinary product topology. Suppose $\alpha:S^{n-1}\to A$, $\beta:D^n\to B$ and $h:S^{n-1}\times[0,1]\to B$ are continuous and satisfy $h(s,0)=w(\alpha(s))$ and $h(s,1)=\beta(s)$. Then there exist continuous maps $\widetilde\alpha:D^n\to A$ and $\widetilde h:D^n\times[0,1]\to B$ satisfying $\widetilde\alpha|_{S^{n-1}}=\alpha$, $\widetilde h|_{S^{n-1}\times[0,1]}=h$, $\widetilde h(x,0)=w(\widetilde\alpha(x))$ and $\widetilde h(x,1)=\beta(x)$ for all $x\in D^n$. No basepoint is fixed, and $A,B$ need not be CW complexes.

source.place: Lemma 3.6.3.11 (Kerodon Tag 0140), proof: the single-cell extension problem and its displayed singular mapping-path lifting square, with the concluding trivial-Kan-fibration argument. This is only the local disk assertion used there, not the whole CW-source conclusion. Transfer the simplex/boundary pair to the Euclidean disk/boundary pair. Weak equivalence is expanded by Remark 3.6.3.4 (013T). Read online 2026-10-17; archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag is claimed for this topological lemma.

proof.text: First pass to k-spaces without imposing any hypothesis on $A,B$. For a topological space $T$, let $kT$ be its underlying set with the final topology for all continuous maps from compact Hausdorff spaces into $T$, using the k-space convention of [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits]. Every such test map is still continuous into $kT$, and $kT\to T$ is continuous. Thus the maps from any compact Hausdorff $C$ into $T$ and into $kT$ are exactly the same. The same test maps define $k(kT)$, so $kT$ is a k-space. More generally a continuous map from a k-space $Z$ into $T$ is continuous into $kT$: compose with every compact Hausdorff test into $Z$ and use the final topology of $Z$. In particular $w$ induces a continuous $w':kA\to kB$. Cubes, their boundaries, and their products with $[0,1]$ are compact Hausdorff; therefore kification changes neither the based maps nor their based homotopies, nor paths or their homotopies. Hence $w'$ has exactly the component bijection and based-group isomorphisms assumed for $w$. The given $\alpha,\beta,h$ also lift, with the same underlying functions, to $kA,kB$.

source.place: Definition 2.4.21 and Proposition 2.4.22; elementary final-topology argument, also used in the proof of Theorem 2.4.23

proof.text: Put $I=[0,1]$. We will use ordinary products with $I$. If $Z$ is a k-space, then $Z\times I$ with its ordinary topology is a k-space. Here is the continuity check, using [lem-coef-compact-open-currying]. Single-point tests first ensure that every slice being transposed is continuous. For any function $F:Z\times I\to T$, continuity of every $F\circ(c\times\mathrm{id}_I)$, for compact Hausdorff tests $c:C\to Z$, implies continuity of every $F^\sharp\circ c:C\to\operatorname{Cont}(I,T)$ by currying. The final topology of $Z$ makes $F^\sharp$ continuous, and evaluation then makes $F$ continuous. Each $C\times I$ is compact Hausdorff, so these compact tests suffice to give the k-space condition. Consequently no k-product replaces the ordinary interval product anywhere below.

source.place: Proposition 2.4.22, with the locally compact exponential law from the opening of section 2.4; the interval-product consequence is proved here

proof.text:
Construct the ordinary topological subspace
$$E_0=\{(a,\gamma)\in kA\times\operatorname{Cont}(I,kB):\gamma(0)=w'(a)\},\qquad E=kE_0,$$
where the function space has the compact-open topology of [lem-coef-compact-open-currying]. Write $q:E\to kA$ for the first projection and $p:E\to kB$ for $(a,\gamma)\mapsto\gamma(1)$. Evaluation is continuous by that node, so these maps are continuous. Define $i:kA\to E$ by $i(a)=(a,\operatorname{const}_{w'(a)})$. The constant-path coordinate is continuous by currying $(a,t)\mapsto w'(a)$; hence $i$ is continuous into $E_0$, and into $E$ by the k-space test from step 1. We have $qi=\mathrm{id}_{kA}$ and $pi=w'$.

source.place: Section 2.4 exponential law and Proposition 2.4.22; explicit topological mapping-path construction, in place of the simplicial construction in Kerodon 0140

proof.text:
The map $i$ is a homotopy equivalence with inverse $q$. The nonconstant homotopy is
$$R:E\times I\to E,\qquad R((a,\gamma),u)=(a,t\mapsto\gamma(ut)).$$
Evaluation and currying [lem-coef-compact-open-currying] make $R$ continuous into $E_0$. Step 2 says $E\times I$ is a k-space, so step 1 makes it continuous into $E=kE_0$. Its endpoints are $R(-,0)=iq$ and $R(-,1)=\mathrm{id}_E$; $qi=\mathrm{id}_{kA}$ has the constant homotopy. Apply [lem-coef-homotopy-equivalence-weak] with $f=i$, $g=q$, the constant homotopy on $kA$, and $R$ on $E$. It follows that $i$ induces the required bijection on path components and all based-group isomorphisms. This invocation allows moving basepoints and empty spaces.

source.place: Section 2.4; explicit mapping-path deformation. Weak-equivalence consequence uses the separate cited homotopy-equivalence theorem

proof.text:
Verify directly that $p$ is a Serre fibration, in the sense of [lem-coef-topological-serre-model]. Suppose $z\mapsto(a_z,\gamma_z)$ is a continuous map $D^m\to E$ and $b:D^m\times I\to kB$ is continuous with $b(z,0)=\gamma_z(1)$. For $z\in D^m$ and $u,t\in I$, set
$$\eta_{z,u}(t)=\begin{cases}\gamma_z((1+u)t)&(1+u)t\leq1,\\ b(z,(1+u)t-1)&(1+u)t\geq1.\end{cases}$$
On the first closed piece, $0\leq(1+u)t\leq1$; on the second, $0\leq(1+u)t-1\leq u\leq1$. Thus both arguments lie in the specified interval domains. The two formulas agree where $(1+u)t=1$, since $\gamma_z(1)=b(z,0)$. They are continuous on two closed subsets covering $D^m\times I\times I$, by evaluation and the assumed continuity of $b$. Their union is continuous: preimages of any closed set are unions of the two closed preimages, proving the finite closed-pasting assertion directly. Curry in $t$ using [lem-coef-compact-open-currying]. Since $D^m\times I$ is compact Hausdorff, step 1 upgrades the resulting map $(z,u)\mapsto(a_z,\eta_{z,u})$ from $E_0$ to $E$. At $u=0$ it is the specified map into $E$ (the second formula only occurs at $t=1$); its final evaluation is $b(z,u)$ and its initial evaluation is $w'(a_z)$. This is the required lift for every $m\geq0$, with no division by $u$ at zero.

source.place: Section 2.4, definition of Serre fibration preceding Theorem 2.4.19 and Theorem 2.4.23; explicit path-concatenation lift supplied here

proof.text: Use [lem-coef-topological-serre-model] in $\mathcal K$. By steps 1 and 4, $w'$ and $i$ are weak equivalences, and $pi=w'$. Two-out-of-three gives that $p$ is a weak equivalence. Step 5 gives that it is also a Serre fibration, so $p\in F\cap W$. Every sphere-boundary inclusion $j:S^{n-1}\hookrightarrow D^n$, including $\varnothing\hookrightarrow D^0$, is one of the generating cofibrations stated in that node and therefore belongs to $C={}^{\pitchfork}(F\cap W)$. Thus every commutative square with $j$ on the left and $p$ on the right admits a continuous diagonal filler in $\mathcal K$.

source.place: Theorem 2.4.23, its generating cofibrations and trivial-fibration lifting property; also Theorem 2.4.19

proof.text:
The lifted boundary data define
$$c:S^{n-1}\to E,\qquad c(s)=(\alpha(s),t\mapsto h(s,t)).$$
The map $c$ is continuous into $E_0$ by [lem-coef-compact-open-currying] and the initial-endpoint condition; it is continuous into $E$ because its domain is compact Hausdorff. Its final evaluation is $pc(s)=h(s,1)=\beta(s)$. Therefore $c$ and $\beta:D^n\to kB$ form the square to which step 6 applies. Obtain $L:D^n\to E$ with $L|_{S^{n-1}}=c$ and $pL=\beta$. For $n=0$ the same argument uses the unique empty boundary map and the generating cofibration $\varnothing\to D^0$; it does not assume a boundary point exists.

source.place: Theorem 2.4.23 lifting property, applied to the prescribed boundary homotopy of Kerodon 0140

proof.text: Write $L(x)=(\widetilde\alpha(x),\gamma_x)$ and set $\widetilde h(x,t)=\gamma_x(t)$. The first coordinate and the map $D^n\to\operatorname{Cont}(I,kB)$ are continuous. Evaluation [lem-coef-compact-open-currying] makes $\widetilde h:D^n\times I\to kB$ continuous with its ordinary product topology. Compose with the continuous identities $kA\to A$, $kB\to B$. The equality $L|_{S^{n-1}}=c$ gives $\widetilde\alpha(s)=\alpha(s)$ and $\widetilde h(s,t)=h(s,t)$ pointwise. Membership in $E_0$ gives $\widetilde h(x,0)=w(\widetilde\alpha(x))$, and $pL=\beta$ gives $\widetilde h(x,1)=\beta(x)$. These are all the required equalities, with no replacement of the prescribed boundary homotopy by a homotopic one.

The delivery is one commit with two files (item and report), no new nodes and no unit-record changes. The statement is unchanged. It matches the single-cell problem in the proof of Kerodon Tag 0140 (Lemma 3.6.3.11), which I read online: a boundary map plus a prescribed boundary homotopy, extended over a simplex, here moved to the disk/sphere pair via the homeomorphism in lem-coef-realization-finite-limits. The weak-equivalence hypothesis is the all-basepoints form of Tag 013T. The statement is true; it is the classical homotopy extension and lifting property for the disk and its boundary sphere. I tested n=0, n=1, empty A or B and non-Hausdorff spaces and found no counterexample. I checked every step. Step 1: kification keeps all compact Hausdorff test maps, so path components, homotopy groups and the weak equivalence are unchanged. Step 2: currying over the locally compact interval shows the ordinary product with the interval is a k-space (Sierpinski-indicator form). Step 3: the mapping-path space E, q, p and i are continuous, with qi=id and pi=w'. Step 4: the deformation R has endpoints iq and id, and lem-coef-homotopy-equivalence-weak applies exactly with f=i, g=q and H constant. Step 5: the piecewise path agrees where the pieces meet, stays in the interval, equals the old path at u=0 and ends at b(z,u), so p is a Serre fibration in the model node's sense. Step 6: two-out-of-three gives p in F∩W. Each sphere-to-disk inclusion is a generating cofibration and so lies in C; this uses the standard meaning of 'generating', which the node does not spell out. Steps 7–8: the square and the evaluation identities check pointwise. proof_deps equals the union of the step uses. By transitive closure on the snapshot, none of the five cited nodes reaches the item, so there is no cycle. No duplicate in the DAG and no SGA source.
